Data companion · Patent institutions

Irish patents and patent institutions

Ireland retained a separate patent system until 1852. These figures examine who used it, what they patented, and how Irish patenting compared with Great Britain before and after unification.

01 / Institutions

A separate system until 1852

Before 1852, protection in Ireland had to be obtained through the Irish patent system. The Patent Law Amendment Act of 1852 brought the separate systems into a common UK framework. This institutional change also affects how the surviving evidence should be read: a series based on English patents before 1852 does not capture patents obtained only in Ireland.

The two datasets presented here answer different questions. The comparative series measures patenting by Irish- and British-domiciled patentees relative to population. The Irish register records patents obtained through the separate Irish system, including those involving patentees domiciled elsewhere. Patenting in Ireland and patenting by Irish residents are therefore distinct measures.

02 / Comparison

Irish patenting in British perspective

The comparative series places Irish patenting alongside Great Britain on a common population basis. The 1852 boundary marks both institutional reform and a change in the geographical coverage of the patent records; changes across it cannot be attributed to reform alone.

03 / The Irish system

Who used the Irish patent system?

The Irish register was used overwhelmingly by patentees domiciled outside Ireland. Between 1800 and 1852, it contains 1,670 patent–patentee entries, of which 77 record an Irish domicile. These entries measure participation in the Irish system, rather than the number of distinct inventions.

What is being counted?

The complete register covers 1708–1852 and contains 1,718 patent–patentee entries. The annual chart shows the 1,670 entries dated 1800–1852. A patent with two patentees contributes two entries, and a person appears again for each patent.

The topic comparison below instead groups entries using the supplied patent number. This produces 1,496 numbered records plus one unnumbered patent, giving 1,497 records. It is a count of register records, not a reconstruction of invention families.

04 / Patent topics

Different patterns of invention

Transportation accounts for 20 of the 73 patents involving an Irish-domiciled patentee (27.4 per cent), compared with 11.7 per cent among patents involving only patentees domiciled elsewhere. Textiles account for a smaller share of the Irish group: 13.7 per cent, against 20.8 per cent. These are differences in the composition of patents obtained through the Irish system, rather than measures of technological quality or invention across the economy.

Why these categories, and how were patents classified?

We use the twenty classes defined by Billington and Hanna (2021, Table 7). Their taxonomy draws on 35 existing classification schemes, review by an experienced patent examiner, and topic analysis across patent datasets. Designed around inventions’ principal economic application, it provides a published basis for comparison and was applied by its authors to British patents from 1700 to 1850.

We applied their definitions to the Irish register descriptions using AI-assisted coding and review. Each patent receives one primary class; all twenty classes are retained. This applies their taxonomy rather than replicating their topic-modelling procedure. The assignments remain provisional, and the catalogue records the reasoning behind them.

Domicile, joint patentees and data checks

Seventy patents involve only Irish-domiciled patentees and three involve both Irish and other domiciles. These form the Irish group of 73. A further 1,422 involve only recorded domiciles elsewhere. Two have no recorded domicile and are omitted from the comparison. No patent is counted in both comparison groups.

The unnumbered record for James Blyth Waynman (1826, “Hat bodies”) is retained separately. Record 13030 has two years, 1849 and 1850, attached to the same description under different patentees. Both years are retained; the patent is counted once in the pooled topic comparison. One patent changes the Irish group’s share by approximately 1.37 percentage points.

06 / Sources and methods

Sources & downloads

The figures use data provided by Stephen Billington, presented and analysed by Christopher L. Colvin and Eoin McLaughlin. Their coverage and units differ; the Irish-register totals should not be added to the comparative series.

  1. Billington, Stephen D., and Alan J. Hanna (2021). “That’s Classified! Inventing a New Patent Taxonomy.” Industrial and Corporate Change, 30(3), 678–705. doi:10.1093/icc/dtaa049. Category definitions: Table 7.
  2. Irish patent register. Complete register of Irish patents, 1708–1852, provided by Stephen Billington, with patentees, domiciles and descriptions. The annual chart and topic classification are derived from this sheet.
  3. Comparative patenting series. Annual patentees per 1,000 persons, 1800–1899. For the underlying British patent dataset, see Berkes, Chen and Tranchero, 300 years of British patents.
  4. Patent Law Amendment Act 1852. 15 & 16 Vict. c. 83. Original Act.

The comparative CSV preserves blank observations as missing values. The classification download retains the two records with unrecorded domicile and the unresolved year discrepancy. The method file documents the counting rules and classification decisions.
